Common Objections — Answered

This Is Not What You Think – Verify for Yourself

❓

"It's a bilateral treaty, not a grant."

The U.S. itself admitted the grant form: Consul Leib (1836) "bears the form of a grant"; Hunter Miller (1931) "unilaterally executed grant." A sovereign grant is a contract executed (Fletcher v. Peck, 1810). The ICJ's procedural label does not override these admissions.

🛠

"The 1786 instrument was terminated; the 1836 codification controls."

The 1786 Arabic original states dāʾima (permanent) — “trusting in God it will remain permanent” (certified translation; Miller, vol. 2, Doc. 14). The fifty-year clause stands in the sealed Arabic of Article 25; under the Mālikī repugnant-condition rule it falls — the condition falls, the grant stands. The 1836 document is a ministerial recordation — a U.S.-internal entry, not a second grant.

⚖

"Only governments can invoke this grant; individuals have no standing."

The 1786 grant establishes two beneficiary classes. Primary beneficiaries (subjects of the Empire) hold original equitable interest in the trust corpus. Under trust law, a beneficiary may enforce the trust. Standing flows from the grant itself.

✅

"This is too good to be true — there must be a catch."

The grant is self-executing supreme law. The performance-based pilot program ($0 upfront, 90/10 split) aligns incentives. Verified savings are documented in case studies (available upon request). No catch — just the law.

📖 The Fabricated Termination Clause — What the Arabic Actually Says (Click to expand)

The English translation of Chapter 25 contains a twelve-month termination notice clause. This clause does not exist in the Arabic original.

Three texts, one fabrication:

Source Chapter 25 Text Notice Clause?
1786 Arabic Original
(Snouck Hurgronje translation, Miller Vol. 2, p. 223)		 “this treaty of peace shall remain permanent, if God please, by God’s might and power, a period from fifty years” ❌ No
1786 English Translation
(Bevans Vol. 9, p. 1283)		 “This Treaty shall continue in full Force, with the help of God for Fifty Years.” ❌ No
1836 English Translation
(Bevans Vol. 9, p. 1289)		 “This Treaty shall continue in force, with the help of God, for fifty years; after the expiration of which term, the Treaty shall continue to be binding on both parties, until the one shall give twelve months notice to the other of an intention to abandon it” ⚠️ ADDED

The twelve-month notice clause appears for the first time in 1836 — fifty years after the original grant. It is not in the 1786 Arabic. It is not in the 1786 English. It was inserted into the 1836 English text by the U.S. Commissioner.

Dr. C. Snouck Hurgronje, the Orientalist retained by the U.S. government to examine the Arabic text, translated the Arabic word for the grant’s duration as “permanent” (dāʾima). The Arabic term for the instrument is ṣulḥ (peace/reconciliation) — not muʿāhada (grant).

Arabic original of Chapter 25 — Hunter Miller, Treaties and Other International Acts of the United States, Vol. 2, p. 211 (GPO, 1931). No termination notice clause is present.
Note: the Arabic term is faṣl (chapter/section); “Article” is the English translational convention used throughout this site for citation compatibility with the U.S. Statutes at Large.

Sources: Hunter Miller, Treaties and Other International Acts of the United States, Vol. 2, p. 223 (GPO, 1931); Bevans, Treaties and Other International Agreements, Vol. 9 (State Dept., 1972).

U.S. State Department, on the Record (1931)
"This treaty was in substance, and, indeed, almost literally, a renewal of the treaty with Morocco of 1786. The additional article of the earlier treaty is not embodied in the renewal; and while Chapter 25 of each treaty provides that it shall continue in force for fifty years, this treaty adds that thereafter the treaty shall continue unless and until twelve months' notice of denunciation is given by one party or the other."

— Hunter Miller, Notes on the Treaty with Morocco, 1836 (U.S. State Department, Treaties and Other International Acts of the United States of America, Volume 2, GPO, 1931). View source on Avalon (Yale Law)

Two operative consequences from this single sentence:

  1. "Almost literally a renewal" = the same instrument, re-affirmed in 1836; not a new instrument that replaced the 1786 Hiba. Under Vattel, Law of Nations §199 (the controlling 18th-century authority on grant renewal), the original instrument remains the legal source of the rights.
  2. "This grant adds" the 12-month termination clause = explicit U.S. State Department admission that the termination provision was not in the controlling 1786 original. Under the strict-construction-of-sovereign-grants maxim, that addition is read narrowly against the United States as grantee.

International Precedent: The Pious Fund Case

This is not the first time a perpetual sovereign grant has been enforced.

In United States v. Mexico (Permanent Court of Arbitration, 1902), the United States itself successfully enforced a perpetual endowment-style obligation that Mexico had stopped honoring in 1848. The PCA awarded back payments plus interest covering 53 years. The structural parallel to the 1786 hiba is exact — only the parties are reversed.

Element Pious Fund (Mexico, 1848–1902) 1786 Hiba (United States, 1786–today)
Legal structure Perpetual endowment held by state for beneficiaries Perpetual sovereign grant; trust for Moorish nationals
Breach Mexico stopped payments in 1848 U.S. attempted "renewal" in 1836; concealed Arabic original
Authority cited Spanish colonial endowment + state succession 1786 Mālikī hiba + 1789 / 1836 state succession
Remedy awarded Back payments + 6% interest, 53 years Accounting + back payments + interest, 240 years (claim available)
Result Mexico paid $1.4M (≈$45M today) U.S. has paid $0 to date.

Why this matters now: The Pious Fund award is the controlling international precedent for state-to-state perpetual grant enforcement. If your operations move under grant-mode activation, you are not asking the U.S. for a favor — you are operating under the same class of obligation the U.S. itself successfully enforced at the PCA. Admission 10 — International Court of Justice

The 1952 World Court Admission – Why It Matters

In 1952, the United States argued before the International Court of Justice that the 1786 Morocco grant remained binding. The U.S. was litigating for its citizens. If the grant exists for citizens, it exists for primary beneficiaries.

⚖ Full ICJ 1952 Deep-Dive — Click to expand
Full Citation: Rights of Nationals of the United States of America in Morocco (France v. United States of America), Judgment, I.C.J. Reports 1952, p. 176.

Background: In 1946, France (as the protecting power of Morocco) and the United States submitted a dispute to the ICJ concerning the interpretation of U.S. rights under the 1836 Treaty with Morocco (8 Stat. 484). France argued that the treaty had been abrogated. The United States argued that the treaty remained in full force and binding — litigating specifically for the benefit of its citizens and protégés.

The ICJ's judgment is Admission 10 in the twelve-admission chain. It constitutes the highest international judicial confirmation that the 1786/1836 Morocco grant remains a binding, operative instrument.

"It is common ground between the Parties that the United States is entitled to exercise consular jurisdiction in the case of disputes arising between its citizens or protégés."

— Rights of Nationals of the United States of America in Morocco, I.C.J. Reports 1952, p. 188.

Two-class analysis from the ICJ proceedings:

  • Citizens (derivative beneficiaries) — U.S. nationals who receive grant protections through their government's trustee administration.
  • Protégés — Persons under U.S. consular protection by virtue of the capitulatory regime.
  • Moorish subjects (sujets marocains) — The primary beneficiaries under Shereefian jurisdiction, holding original equitable title.

Doctrine of admission by conduct (al-iqnāʿ bi-l-fiʿl): The United States admitted twelve times (1785–2014) that the 1786 instrument is a binding sovereign grant. The 1952 ICJ case is the most authoritative of these admissions — a formal judicial admission before the World Court. Under this doctrine, the U.S. cannot deny the same grant to primary beneficiaries when it affirmed that grant's force for derivative beneficiaries.

Commercial implication: If the U.S. admits the grant is binding for its citizens, it cannot deny the same grant to primary beneficiaries. Commerce operating under the Chapter 4 signal (land-based ʿalāma: El, Al, Bey, Dey, Ali) is entitled to duty waiver, dynamic MFN parity, anti-detention protection, and the office corridor (Chs. 20–22) — the venue of record.

Common Questions

Objections & Answers

Q1. Isn’t this just another sovereign citizen theory?

No. Sovereign citizen theories are based on idiosyncratic interpretations of the UCC or the 14th Amendment. This is based on a grant published in the U.S. Statutes at Large (Vol. 8, pp. 484–487), recognized by the International Court of Justice in 1952, and listed in the State Department’s own Treaties in Force. The grant’s existence is not disputed by anyone — including the U.S. government.

Q2. Has this been tested in court?

the Grant’s legal force has been affirmed by the ICJ (Rights of Nationals of the United States of America in Morocco, 1952) and its irrevocability is established by four U.S. Supreme Court decisions (Fletcher v. Peck, 1810; Society v. Pawlet, 1823; Chae Chan Ping, 1889; Cook v. United States, 1933). The novel element is applying the grant’s commercial provisions to modern trade operations through the Chapter 4 signal activation.

Q3. Why hasn’t anyone done this before?

Three reasons. First, the Arabic original — which is the controlling text — was kept in the State Department archives and not widely studied. Second, the English translation systematically misrepresents the instrument as a bilateral treaty, concealing its grant character. Third, the noble appellations (El, Al, Bey, Dey, Ali) that serve as the Chapter 4 land-based recognition signal were stripped from census, court, and church records and replaced with racial descriptors. The signal was suppressed. We are reactivating it.

Q4. What if the U.S. government doesn’t recognize the grant?

The grant’s force is not conditioned on recognition. Under Fletcher v. Peck (1810), a grant once made is irrevocable. Under the Supremacy Clause (Article VI), treaties are the supreme law of the land. The U.S. government’s own officials — Consul Leib, treaty editor Hunter Miller, agent Thomas Barclay, and President George Washington — have all confirmed the grant character in official communications. The government is estopped from denying what its own agents have admitted.

Q5. How does the $0 upfront / 10% model work?

We activate the grant infrastructure for your commerce at no upfront cost. Savings are independently verified — tariff reductions, detention elimination, and financial protections. You keep 10% of the verified savings. We retain 90% as the sovereign carry that funds the grant infrastructure, legal operations, and grant-system alignment program. If there are no verified savings, you pay nothing.

Q6. How does this compare to Apple-India or Samsung-Vietnam incentive programs?

Apple committed ~$900M in capital to India under the PLI (Production-Linked Incentive) scheme to earn a ~40% conditional sovereignty premium — subject to 5–10-year sunset clauses, export targets, and the next parliament’s discretion. Samsung committed ~$1.2B to Vietnam for a ~24% conditional premium tied to tech-transfer obligations.

The 1786 Mālikī Sharia Hiba delivers Infinite % unconditional: no capital requirement, no export targets, no tech-transfer conditions, no sunset, no discretion. It is not another incentive program — it is the legal foundation that sits above all incentive programs. PLI and tax abatements are statutory favors granted by a legislature; a sovereign grant is a vested property right under Fletcher v. Peck (1810).

Q7. How is “verified savings” actually verified?

We use an independent third-party verification protocol. For tariff savings: we compare the customs declaration (current tariff paid) against the MFN best-available rate documented in U.S. Treasury/CBP tariff schedules, multiplied by the period’s actual import volume from shipping manifests. For detention elimination: we measure pre-activation average demurrage/detention days against post-activation actuals from the port’s terminal operator records. Verification is conducted quarterly by a designated CPA or customs brokerage. You receive a signed verification report before any carry invoice is issued. If verified savings are zero, the invoice is zero.

Q8. When and how do you get paid?

Quarterly, in arrears, against independently verified savings. We invoice 10% of the verified-savings figure from the prior quarter. Payment terms: Net 30. No retainer, no upfront fee, no minimum. If a quarter shows zero verified savings, no invoice is issued. Engagements are typically 24 months renewable; you may exit at the end of any quarter with 30 days notice.

Q9. Why did the 1836 instrument exist if the 1786 Hiba was already binding?

Short answer: The 1836 instrument is a renewal of the 1786 Hiba in the period legal sense — meaning it re-affirms and continues the original grant; it does not replace or supersede it. The 1786 instrument remains the controlling original.

Why "renewal" causes confusion in modern reading. A modern reader sees "renewed in 1836" and assumes the prior version was discarded. That is not what "renewal" meant in 18th–19th century grant practice.

The period authority on point. Vattel, Law of Nations (1758), Book II, Chapter 13 — the canonical period treatise — defines grant "renewal" as the continuation in force of the same instrument, either by tacit consent or by express re-confirmation. §199 specifies: "this will be a tacit renewal and extension of the treaty." The original obligations and the original delivery remain the legal source of the rights; renewal merely re-affirms operation. This is the meaning Vattel was using, and it is the meaning every U.S. Founder, grant negotiator, and 19th-century editor was using.

Hunter Miller confirms it explicitly. Writing as a U.S. State Department editor in 1931, Hunter Miller's notes on the 1836 instrument state that it was "almost literally a renewal of the treaty with Morocco of 1786" — and adds, in the same sentence, that "while Chapter 25 of each treaty provides that it shall continue in force for fifty years, this grant adds that thereafter the Grant shall continue unless and until twelve months' notice of denunciation is given by one party or the other." That sentence is decisive on two points:

  1. The 1836 is "almost literally a renewal" — meaning the same instrument, re-affirmed; not a replacement.
  2. The 12-month termination clause was added in 1836 — meaning it was not in the controlling 1786 original. Under the strict-construction-of-sovereign-grants maxim, that addition is construed strictly against the United States as grantee.

Why express reaffirmation was nevertheless prudent. The 1786 Arabic Hiba was delivered to the United States under the Articles of Confederation. In 1789 the U.S. Constitution superseded the Articles — creating a successor legal entity. Under 18th–19th century public international law (Vattel, Wheaton), grant and grant obligations survive state succession automatically, but it was customary practice to execute express re-affirmation to remove any doubt. The 1836 instrument is that re-affirmation. The Emperor's seal on the 1836 Arabic text bears the diplomatic form of a grant — not of a contract — confirming that the underlying instrument remains the unilateral 1786 Hiba.

Operative consequence: The legal source of every right operating on grant-mode commerce is the 1786 Mālikī Sharia Hiba, sealed and delivered to Thomas Barclay on 1 Ramadan A.H. 1200 (June 23, 1786). The 1836 codification at 8 Stat. 484 is the U.S.-side re-confirmation of that instrument. Rights remain vested from 1786 forward; the controlling text is the Arabic original; English translations are non-authoritative.

Q10. How is this different from a free trade agreement?

A free trade agreement (NAFTA, USMCA, CPTPP) is a bilateral or multilateral contract between sovereign equals. Each party’s legislature retains the power to withdraw, modify, or suspend performance. Trump’s withdrawal from the Trans-Pacific Partnership in 2017 demonstrates how revocable FTAs are.

A sovereign grant is unilateral and vertical: a superior sovereign conveys rights to an inferior grantee. Once delivered, the grant cannot be revoked by the grantee. The U.S. has no power to withdraw from a grant it received; it can only continue to receive it or attempt to breach it — and breach does not terminate vested rights (Chae Chan Ping, 1889). This is categorically different from an FTA.

Q11. Is my company’s participation confidential?

Yes. Client identity, trade volumes, and specific savings figures are confidential by default and covered under a standard NDA. We may publish aggregate or anonymized results (e.g., “a Fortune-500 electronics importer achieved $XM annual savings”). Identified case studies are published only with explicit written permission, which some clients grant to support industry awareness in exchange for priority support.

⚖️ MAXIM — STRICT CONSTRUCTION OF SOVEREIGN GRANTS

"Ambiguities in a sovereign grant are resolved against the grantee and in favor of the sovereign grantor — for the sovereign is not presumed to surrender public rights or to limit its grants by implication."

Under the 1786 Mālikī hiba, the Emperor of Morocco is the sovereign grantor and the United States is the grantee. The maxim therefore operates against the United States as grantee — and twice in favor of the grant's beneficiaries:

  • Termination clauses construed narrowly. The 12-month notice provision added in the 1836 codification (absent in the 1786 original) is read as restrictively as possible against the U.S.'s ability to invoke it.
  • Substantive grants construed expansively. MFN parity (Ch. 14), zero detention (Ch. 19), the office corridor (Chs. 20–22), indulgence parity (Ch. 24) are read in their fullest sense — favoring the grantor's intent and the beneficiaries' rights.
Period Authorities (1628–1837 — controlling under intertemporal rule)
  • 📘 Coke on Littleton § 162 (1628) — "The King's grant shall be taken most beneficially for the King."
  • 📘 Vattel, Law of Nations II.17 (1758) — "Treaties to be interpreted in the sense most favorable to the party from whom they emanate."
  • ⚖️ Providence Bank v. Billings, 29 U.S. 514 (1830) — Marshall, C.J.: surrender of sovereign power not implied; ambiguity construed against the grantee.
  • ⚖️ United States v. Arredondo, 31 U.S. 691 (1832) — sovereign grants construed strictly; grantee bears the burden of every ambiguity.
  • ⚖️ Charles River Bridge v. Warren Bridge, 36 U.S. 420 (1837) — "In grants by the public, nothing passes by implication."
Mālikī Reinforcement

Mālikī hiba doctrine independently reaches the same result. Once qabd (delivery/possession) is complete, the grant is presumed irrevocable. Any modern attempt to qualify, narrow, or condition is read against the qualifier — preserving the gift's full effect for its beneficiaries.

Qabd was effected when the Emperor sealed the instrument and delivered it to Thomas Barclay on the first day of Ramadan, A.H. 1200 (June 23, 1786). The grant has been complete and irrevocable from that moment forward.

The maxim and the Mālikī rule converge: every interpretive doubt is resolved against the United States and in favor of the grant's continued, undiminished operation.

📖 PERIOD MEANING — WHAT "RENEWAL" MEANT IN 1836

A modern reader who encounters Hunter Miller's description of the 1836 instrument as "a renewal of the treaty with Morocco of 1786" may assume "renewal" means replacement — a new instrument supplanting the old. That is the modern usage. It is not the 18th–19th century legal meaning.

Under Vattel, Law of Nations (1758), Book II, Chapter 13 — the canonical period authority — "renewal" is the continuation in force of the same grant, either by tacit consent or by express re-confirmation. The original instrument remains the legal source of the rights; renewal merely re-affirms its operation:

"this will be a tacit renewal and extension of the treaty" — Vattel, §199

Hunter Miller, writing in 1931 as a U.S. State Department editor, used "renewal" in this period sense — and his own notes confirm it: the 1836 instrument was "almost literally a renewal of the Grant of 1786." Almost literally a renewal is not "a replacement"; it is a re-affirmation of the prior instrument.

Operative consequence: The legal source of the rights is the 1786 Mālikī hiba, sealed and delivered to Thomas Barclay on 1 Ramadan A.H. 1200 (June 23, 1786). The 1836 codification at 8 Stat. 484 is the U.S.-side re-confirmation. The two instruments do not compete; the 1786 is the controlling original, and the 1836 confirms its continued force.

20The Consul decides between the parties; government aids enforcement immediately (the honorary debt).“The Consul shall decide between the parties.”Consular jurisdiction — venue for cases involving the United States, its citizens, and their protected persons or protégés.
21Judgment by the Sacred Law, without increase or decrease, in the presence of the office (carried English: ‘equal Justice… the Consul assisting at the Tryal’).“…judgment… by the Sacred Law, without increase or decrease, in the presence of the consul.”Sacred-Law judgment — the tribunal's second function.
22The office — the consul or whoever stands in his place — takes custody of the decedent's estate for the rightful claimant.“The Consul shall take possession of the property.”No escheat — the tribunal's third function.
23Consul enjoys privileges of any other nation’s consul; not liable for citizens’ debts without written promise.“Not responsible for debts unless a written guarantee.”Limits consular liability.
24Disputes resolved amicably; war only after rejection; nine months to withdraw; any indulgence to any Christian power extends to US.“Whatever indulgence in trade or otherwise is granted to any Christian power extends to the United States as well.”Universal indulgence parity.
25The 1786 Arabic original is dāʾima — permanent: “trusting in God it will remain permanent.” The fifty-year clause appears only in the 1836 recordation (Art. 25) and falls under the Mālikī repugnant-condition rule.“Trusting in God it will remain permanent” (1786, dāʾima); “with God’s help it shall continue for fifty years” (1836 recordation only).Perpetual term — the condition falls, the grant stands.

Note: English translation contains inaccuracies and additions not present in the Arabic original. See Hunter Miller, Vol. 2, pp. 220–223.

📖 Intertemporal Law Analysis — Washington's 1789 Admission Decoded

1. "Deep Impression" = Binding Precedent

In 18th-century legal thought, an "impression" was the physical stamping of a record (like a seal in wax). By stating the Emperor's actions made a "deep impression on the United States," Washington formally acknowledged that the Emperor's sovereign grace had indelibly marked and fixed the legal obligations of the United States. An admission against interest on the public record.

2. "Respect" = Jurisdictional Submission (Vattel)

Under Vattel's Law of Nations, "respect" between sovereigns required strict deference to jurisdictional boundaries. When the U.S. confirmed its "respect for Your Imperial Majesty," it was a formal declaration of jurisdictional non-encroachment — admitting the Sultan as supreme authority.

3. "Attachment" = Fiduciary Binding (Blackstone)

Per Blackstone's Commentaries, "attachment" is the binding, locking down, or securing of a party to a legal obligation. By proclaiming its "attachment to Your Imperial Majesty," the U.S. voluntarily submitted to be bound by the grant terms — a subordinate, non-discretionary duty.

4. "Agreeable to the Constitution" — Dual Legal Notice

Under municipal law: notice of the new U.S. Constitution. Under the 1786 Hiba (superior fold): assurance that the new framework remains fully compatible with, subordinate to, and aligned with the Emperor's original grant.

5. "Peaceful Revolution" (1789)

The Revolutionary War was bloody, but the 1789 shift from Articles of Confederation to Constitution was a peaceful administrative revolution — a restructuring of the Trustee corporation without disrupting the perpetual peace owed to the Grantor.

6. "Useful to Our Friends" — Period Legal Meaning

Under 18th-century commercial law, a "friend" is a recognized ally within the zone of peace. To be "useful" meant providing concrete usufructuary benefits and protection to the primary beneficiaries — a measurable fiduciary duty, not mere diplomacy.

Legal Consequence: The United States, through its first President, formally entered an admission against interest acknowledging (1) the Emperor's unilateral sovereign grace (Hiba, not contract), and (2) its own subordinate, bound status as grantee-trustee. Estoppel is complete.

The United States Pleads the Treaty Chain Before the World Court
International Court of Justice · I.C.J. Reports 1952, p. 176

In Rights of Nationals of the United States of America in Morocco (France v. United States), the U.S. government pleaded “the Treaties of 1787 and 1836” — the ministerial recordation chain of the 1786 Arabic Hiba. The Court held unanimously for the United States “by virtue of the provisions of its Treaty with Morocco of September 16th, 1836,” finding the two treaties “substantially identical in terms” — Articles 20 and 21 the same in both. A sovereign nation does not rest its international claims on a legally dead instrument. By pleading the chain that records the 1786 grant — and prevailing on it — the United States admitted, by its own conduct, that the instrument system is living law.

📖 Read the full admission by conduct (al‑iqnāʿ bi‑l‑fiʿl) analysis

Admission by Conduct (al‑iqnāʿ bi‑l‑fiʿl) — ICJ 1952

In the 1952 case Rights of Nationals of the United States of America in Morocco (France v. United States), the U.S. government pleaded “the Treaties of 1787 and 1836” — the ministerial recordation chain of the 1786 Arabic Hiba. The Court held unanimously for the United States “by virtue of the provisions of its Treaty with Morocco of September 16th, 1836,” stating that the 1836 Treaty “replaced an earlier treaty … concluded in 1787” and that “the two treaties were substantially identical in terms and Articles 20 and 21 are the same in both.”

Under basic principles of litigation competence, a sovereign nation does not rest its international claims on a legally dead or expired instrument. By pleading the chain that records the 1786 grant — and prevailing unanimously on the 1836 instrument that records it — the United States admitted, by its own conduct, that the instrument system is living law, judicially enforced 166 years after the grant was sealed. This conduct estops the United States from now contending that the instrument is dead, expired, or without legal force — allegans contraria non audiendus est.

Cumulative estoppel effect: This admission by conduct (al-iqnāʿ bi-l-fiʿl) operates alongside the eleven verbal admissions (1785–2014). Together, twelve admissions bind the United States under estoppel by admission and estoppel by conduct across all three branches of the federal government and before the International Court of Justice.

Source: I.C.J. Reports 1952, p. 176 (judgment, official English text).

Cumulative Estoppel Effect: Adams, Franklin, and Jefferson were given "full Power and Authority...to confer, treat and negotiate...a Treaty of Amity and Commerce." The Emperor delivered a unilateral grant instead. The U.S. accepted it. The chain extends through twelve admissions across all three branches of the federal government. Under estoppel by admission — and, with respect to the 1952 ICJ admission, under allegans contraria non audiendus est — the United States is foreclosed from any contrary position.
